newsitem.title: UK: British sheep clone raises spectre of Frankenstein.
newsitem.headline: British sheep clone raises spectre of Frankenstein.

text.p: The first-ever cloning of an adult animal -- a sheep named Dolly -- sent a shudder through Britain's scientific establishment on Monday, with one commentator warning that unscrupulous doctors could go on to produce human "Frankensteins."
Ian Wilmut of the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, working with biotechnology company PPL Therapeutics, said on Sunday the female sheep was born seven months ago.

Doctors heralded the achievement as a scientific breakthrough that would help scientists grow herds of transgenic animals that could be farmed for proteins, blood and even organs of medical benefit to humanity.
Wilmut's group, who report their findings in the journal Nature this week, cloned their first sheep last year and excited debate about whether monsters or miracles had been created.
The controversy was re-born on Monday, with images of Aldous Huxley's novel "Brave New World" in which both animals and humans were produced on a eugenic assembly line.
"I would have preferred never to have seen it happen," said Richard Nicholson, editor of the Bulletin of Medical Ethics.

"The problem with all these new scientific techniques (is) once you've published it in an international journal like Nature then it's available to any scientists regardless of how careful they are to practice within moral bounds around the world," he told BBC radio.
"In this country we are probably fairly safe from the Frankenstein factor but the problem is that worldwide we certainly are not."

Dr Patrick Dixon, a writer on genetic matters, said he had been contacted recently by a woman who wanted to clone her dead father. "She wants to bring him back to life as a baby, perhaps even carrying him in her own womb," Dixon told the Times.
"After hearing of Dr Wilmut's progress, I sent her a message today saying it will be possible sooner than she thinks."
Dixon said people with serious diseases could have themselves cloned for spare body parts, dictators could have themselves cloned, or dead film stars could be resurrected in the form of a clone.
Other scientists expressed worries about the scientific safety and noted that many of the animals produced at the Roslin Institute had died with physical defects.
"It's a pretty risky technique with lots of abnormalities," Lewis Wolpert of University College London, chairman of the Committee for Public Understanding of Science, told the Guardian newspaper.

Cloning an adult reproduces all the little mutations that add up over a lifetime, mutations that come from everyday radiation, toxins in the environment, and simple mistakes that creep in every time a cell divides.
But Wilmut defended both the science and the ethics involved.
"We feel that it is important that society is able to consider the potential misuses of this technique and to ensure that legislation is in place to prevent it," he told the BBC.

PPL is in the final stages of testing transgenic sheep that produce milk containing a human protein that can help treat cystic fibrosis, a serious genetic disease causing difficulty breathing, digestive disorders and lung infections.
But the controversy is sure to continue as Europe debates the desirability of genetically engineered organisms, with fears over modified foods such as maize and soya leading the list.
